lines: You have the Python. Every change to it lands as a commit.
So this refresher covers how to reshape that history, how to search it, and how to share it.
All familiar? Swipe on to the shell.
Our repository is a small data cleaning script, and this branch adds deduplication. There are two ways to bring it in.
A merge keeps both lines of history, tied together by a commit with two parents. Nothing is rewritten.
A rebase takes your commits and replays them on top of the target, giving one straight line, as if the work had happened in order.
Rebase the branch onto main. What happens to its commits?
answer: They become three new commits with new identifiers.
A commit's identifier is a hash of its parent, its files, its author and dates, and its message. Replay it on a different parent and the hash has to change.
The old commits are still reachable in the reference log. A merge would have kept them and added one more commit. But look at the end: both routes finish with exactly the same files.

lines: Before you push a branch, you are free to tidy it. An interactive rebase lets you reorder, reword, squash, fix up and drop commits.
A small trick: commit a correction with the fix up option, and the auto squash option moves it directly under the commit it repairs.
Watch the four commits become two, with the debug commit gone.

The rule is simple. Never rewrite what other people have already pulled, because they would have to repair their copy. And your own rewrite is undoable: the old branch is one reference log entry back.
When both sides change the same lines, or lines next to each other, Git stops and keeps three versions of the file.
The common ancestor, yours, and theirs. Turn on the three way conflict style and the file shows the ancestor as well, so you can see what each side actually changed rather than guessing.
Edit, add the file, continue. Or abort to back out completely.
One trap: during a rebase, ours and theirs swap. Ours is the branch you are rebasing onto, and theirs is your own commit being replayed.
Now searching history. Bisect is a binary search over commits: you name one good and one bad, and it checks out the middle for you to test.
Every answer throws away half of the suspects.
With a thousand commits between them, how many tests until it finds the first bad one?
answer: Each test halves the range, and ten halvings take about a thousand down to one. Checking one by one could take nearly a thousand tests.
That is the same logarithm from the last refresher, applied to history instead of data.

lines: Better still, let Git do the testing. Give bisect run a command, and it reads exactly one thing back: the exit status.
Zero means the commit is good. A failure code means it is bad. One special code means this commit cannot be tested, so skip it. Anything else stops the run.
So the best test fails only because of the bug, and it should live outside the repository, otherwise checking out an old commit changes the test itself.
Those exit codes will come back in the next refresher.
A pull request asks for review and automated checks before a branch lands. It can land in three ways.
A merge commit keeps every commit. A squash turns the whole branch into one commit. Rebase and merge replays the commits in a line.
Now a subtle consequence. You squash a three commit request, then add one more commit to the same branch and open a new request.
How many commits does the new request list?
answer: The squash commit is not made of your three commits, so Git still sees those three as unmerged and lists them again, with the new one.
Here they even conflict. So after a squash merge, start a fresh branch from main.

lines: The last point is about branch length, which is the real risk.
In trunk based development everyone merges into one trunk at least daily, through branches that live only long enough to be reviewed and checked.
Bigger changes still land in small steps, hidden behind flags.
A long lived branch drifts. The gap grows every day, so the final merge grows with it, and keeping it current means resolving the same conflicts again and again.
Eight things to keep. Merge keeps both parents. Rebase replays with new identifiers. Rewrite only what you have not pushed.
A conflict has a base, ours and theirs. Bisect finds a bug in about ten tests, and bisect run reads the exit status.
A pull request can land by merge, squash or rebase, and after a squash you retire the branch. And keep your branches short.
Next up: the shell, where those exit codes come from.
